claims.text: A computationally guided metastability-engineering strategy will improve the combined strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance of structural high-entropy alloys.
The proposed starting material is a high-entropy alloy in the as-cast state.
Computational modeling can optimize alloy composition and microstructure to produce a useful metastable state.
The proposed strategy controls grain-boundary segregation.
The proposed strategy controls precipitation of secondary phases.
Control of grain-boundary segregation and secondary-phase precipitation enhances alloy strength.
Control of grain-boundary segregation and secondary-phase precipitation enhances alloy ductility.
Control of grain-boundary segregation and secondary-phase precipitation enhances fracture resistance.
The strategy is expected to increase strength by 20% relative to current high-entropy alloys made by conventional processing.
The strategy is expected to increase ductility by 30% relative to current high-entropy alloys made by conventional processing.
The strategy is expected to increase Young’s modulus by 10% relative to current high-entropy alloys made by conventional processing.
The strategy is expected to increase fracture resistance by 25% relative to current high-entropy alloys made by conventional processing.
The strategy is expected to work at temperatures up to 500°C and stresses up to 1000 MPa.
The strategy may not be effective above 800°C or above 1500 MPa.
The magnitude of improvement depends on the specific alloy composition and microstructure.
The computational modeling requires further validation and refinement.
The hypothesis is falsified if the engineered alloys show less than 10% improvement in at least two measured properties relative to conventionally processed controls.
